stimulus.source_note: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835), Henry Reeve translation; public domain.
stimulus.text: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835), after traveling in the United States: “The first and most intense passion which is engendered by the equality of conditions is, I need hardly say, the love of that same equality.” He added: “The peculiar and preponderating fact which marks those ages as its own is the equality of conditions; the ruling passion of men in those periods is the love of this equality.”

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835), public domain
stem: Tocqueville wrote that democratic peoples love equality more than liberty. Which of the following best explains the tension he saw in American democracy?

options.text: Americans loved equality so much that they abolished slavery throughout the country in the 1830s.
options.misconception: Slavery was not abolished in the 1830s; it grew stronger in the South in those years.

options.text: A majority that loved equality could still deny it to enslaved people, Native peoples, and women.
Americans loved liberty so much that they refused to pay any taxes at all.
options.misconception: Americans paid taxes in the 1830s; love of liberty did not end taxation.

options.text: Equality of conditions meant that every American earned exactly the same wages.
options.misconception: Equality of conditions meant no fixed ranks, not identical wages; rich and poor still existed.

rationales.A: Slavery was not abolished in the 1830s. It grew stronger in the South in those very years.
rationales.B: Tocqueville himself wrote at length about enslaved people and Native peoples. Background: the white majority cherished equality among themselves while denying it to those outside the majority.
rationales.C: Americans paid taxes in the 1830s. Love of liberty did not end taxation.
rationales.D: Equality of conditions meant no fixed ranks, not identical wages. Rich and poor still existed side by side.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who shares the equality. Background: the passion Tocqueville describes belonged to the white men who vote and govern.
2. Ask who is left out. Enslaved people, Native peoples, and women lived under the same laws without the same rights.
3. Ask what the majority does with its power. It can guard its own equality and still deny it to others.
4. Put it together. A democracy can love equality and still draw a hard line around who counts.
Remember: in the 1830s, American equality had a boundary, and the boundary is the story.
